stakeholders.name: high_frequency_traders
stakeholders.situation: Pays a significant premium for co-location services and specialized low-latency infrastructure (e.g., millimeter wave links, straight-line fiber optic cables) to minimize the physical delay between their algorithms and financial exchanges. The speed of light is the ultimate, non-negotiable floor on their ability to execute trades faster than competitors. Exit would mean abandoning their entire business model.

stakeholders.name: cloud_service_providers
stakeholders.situation: Designs and operates global networks of data centers with availability zones and regions. They set the agenda for how the digital world is architected by placing infrastructure strategically to mitigate latency for their customers. They cannot change the speed of light, but they arbitrage geography to sell proximity and performance as a service.

stakeholders.name: distributed_systems_engineers
stakeholders.situation: Develops the architectural patterns (e.g., eventual consistency, CRDTs, CDNs, edge computing) that allow global-scale software to function in the face of unavoidable latency. Their work defines how applications are built to be tolerant of this physical limit. Exit means choosing a different problem space, but within distributed systems, this constraint is a given.

stakeholders.name: data_center_real_estate_developers
stakeholders.situation: Benefits directly from the need to place computational resources physically close to users or other infrastructure. The speed of light creates a durable market for strategically located, high-connectivity real estate in financial hubs and major population centers.

stakeholders.name: global_online_gamers
stakeholders.situation: Experiences the constraint directly as 'lag' or 'high ping,' which degrades or ruins the experience in fast-paced games. They pay this cost in user experience and are a major driver for the development of regional servers and edge computing nodes. They can choose servers closer to them but cannot eliminate the latency to play with friends on other continents.

stakeholders.name: physicists
stakeholders.situation: Studies, measures, and defines the nature of this physical constant. They do not pay its costs or collect its benefits in the same way as other stakeholders, but provide the formal understanding of why the constraint exists and is absolute. Their 'seat' is one of pure observation and theory.

stakeholders.name: future_interplanetary_colonists
stakeholders.situation: A future group whose entire social, political, and technical reality will be defined by this constraint, with communication round-trip times to Earth measured in minutes to hours. They are not present to influence today's long-term communication protocol designs, but they will be the ultimate payers of this latency cost. They are excluded by virtue of not yet existing.

six_questions.coordination_function: Forces the geographic distribution of computational resources and the development of asynchronous communication protocols to allow global systems to function despite inherent, non-negotiable delays.
six_questions.transfer_function: Moves economic value from actors who require low-latency (e.g., traders, gamers, streaming services) to those who can provide physical proximity (e.g., co-location providers, data center real estate, specialized fiber optic network builders).
six_questions.absent_voices: Future inhabitants of a multi-planetary civilization. Their governance, culture, and relationship with Earth will be fundamentally shaped by communication delays of minutes or hours, yet they are not part of any current discussion on building long-term, delay-tolerant communication systems.
six_questions.disappearance_rationale: If faster-than-light communication became possible, the entire economic and architectural basis for distributed systems, CDNs, edge computing, and co-located financial trading would instantly evaporate. A single, centralized global data center would become feasible, erasing trillions of dollars in geographically-distributed infrastructure value and remaking the internet's topology.
six_questions.founding_problem: The constraint is not an 'arrangement' built to solve a problem; it is a fundamental property of physics that all information-transmitting arrangements must contend with. The problem it addresses is simply 'how fast can a cause-and-effect relationship propagate across a distance?'
six_questions.founding_problem_corroboration: The entire field of experimental and theoretical physics, from the Michelson-Morley experiment to Einstein's theory of special relativity and every subsequent empirical test, corroborates that this speed limit is a fundamental and invariant feature of our universe.

commentary.narrative_context: The speed of light in a vacuum (c) represents a hard, physical upper bound on the speed at which information can travel. In practical terms, such as data moving through fiber optic cables, the speed is even lower (around 2/3 c). This creates a minimum, non-zero latency for any communication between two geographically separate points, a delay that is directly proportional to the distance. This physical fact is a fundamental constraint that shapes the architecture of the global internet, financial markets, and all distributed technological systems.
